spec.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on R^n. The finite energy E(t)=∫_{R^n} (|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²) dx is differentiable on (0,∞) and E'(t)=0 for every t>0. In particular E is constant on (0,∞), with exactly this normalization; no assertion at time zero is made.

hypotheses.statement: u:R^n×(0,∞)→R^m is jointly smooth (C^∞ in space and time).
q∈R^m is fixed, independent of space and time, and |q|=1.
For all x∈R^n and all t>0, |u(x,t)|=1.
For each x∈R^n and t>0 there exists a real scalar a such that u_tt(x,t)-Δ_xu(x,t)=a u(x,t). No regularity of a pointwise selection of these scalars is assumed.
For every pair of real numbers 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact set C_[s,t]⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C_[s,t] and every r∈[s,t].

definitions.definition: u_t(x,t)=∂u(x,t)/∂t, the componentwise first time derivative.

definitions.type: family of componentwise spatial differential operators
definitions.definition: For each integer j with 1≤j≤n, ∂_{x_j} denotes componentwise differentiation in the jth spatial coordinate on R^n. Repeated subscripts denote iterated spatial derivatives, and ∂_{x_j}u_t differentiates u_t in that coordinate. Spatial gradients of u have rows ∂_{x_j}u; their Frobenius square is ∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|².

μ is Lebesgue measure on R^n, identified with the product of n one-dimensional Lebesgue measures; dx in spatial integrals denotes dμ. Euclidean dot products and norms are used in R^m and its finite matrix spaces. On coordinate boxes, μ is the product of the restricted coordinate Lebesgue measures.
E(t)=∫_{R^n} e(x,t) dx, with the ordinary finite Lebesgue integral, used only after spatial integrability for every positive time has been proved.

propositions.statement: For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊂R^n and R>0 such that C⊂(-R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and, with Q=[-R,R]^n, μ(Q)=(2R)^n<∞. Every positive-order space/time derivative of u vanishes on (R^n\C)×int(J). The functions e and e_t are smooth. For every r∈int(J), e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j∈{1,…,n}, the functions ∂_{x_j}u(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,r), u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u(·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·∂_{x_j}u(·,r)) are continuous, vanish outside C, and are absolutely integrable on R^n. All these scalar functions are bounded on every compact space-time box Q×K with K a compact subinterval of int(J). In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

For every t>0, E is differentiable at t and E'(t)=∫_{R^n} e_t(x,t) dx=2∫_{R^n} u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t) dx+2∑_{j=1}^n ∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t) dx. Pointwise, e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. All displayed integrals are absolutely finite.
For every t>0 and j∈{1,…,n}, ∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t) dx = -∫_{R^n} u_t(x,t)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t) dx; both integrals are absolutely finite.

In particular E is constant on (0,∞), with exactly this normalization; no assertion at time zero is made.

locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary spatial point x.
At (x,t), choose a satisfying u_tt-Δ_xu=a u, as supplied by H005.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary x∈R^n and t>0. H001 makes the coordinate sums finite, and H002 permits componentwise product rules and equality of mixed derivatives. H004 gives u·u=1. Differentiating in time yields 2u·u_t=0, hence u·u_t=0. Differentiating once more yields 2|u_t|²+2u·u_tt=0, hence u·u_tt=-|u_t|². For each spatial coordinate j=1,…,n, two differentiations of the same unit constraint yield 2|∂_{x_j}u|²+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=0, hence u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|². These are routine product-rule calculations on the open domain R^n×(0,∞).

produces.statement: At the fixed (x,t), u·u_t=0, u·u_tt=-|u_t|², and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|² for every j∈{1,…,n}.

argument.text: Choose the pointwise scalar a from H005. By F001, u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0. Dotting u_tt-Δ_xu=a u with u and using H004 and F001 gives a=u·u_tt-∑_{j=1}^n u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|²-|u_t|². Substitution gives the stated explicit wave-map equation. The same calculation applies to any scalar satisfying the pointwise normality equation, so it also proves the assertion about every such scalar. No derivative or regular selection of a was used. Eliminate this pointwise witness and universally quantify the arbitrary x,t to obtain all asserted tangency identities and the explicit wave-map equation.

locals.declaration: Choose C from H006 for s=t0/2 and t=3t0/2, so u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J.
Choose R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n using F001.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Since 0<t0/2<3t0/2, H006 gives a compact C with u(x,r)=q for x∉C, r∈J. H001 supplies the positive finite spatial dimension. A compact subset of Euclidean space is bounded; choosing a strict larger coordinate bound, there exists R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This standard compactness consequence also covers an empty C (any positive R works).

produces.statement: There exists a positive real R with C⊂(-R,R)^n.

argument.text: Choose R as in F001 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. Its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞, by the product formula for a coordinate box. Compact C is closed; hence (R^n\C)×int(J) is open. On this open set u is the constant vector q: H003 supplies that q is fixed, and H006 supplies the equality. By H002, every positive-order derivative of u therefore vanishes there. In particular e,e_t and the scalar functions u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) for every spatial index j vanish there. Smoothness, finite sums and products also imply their continuity (indeed smoothness). For a fixed r∈int(J), each scalar function is bounded on compact Q and zero off C⊂Q. Its absolute value is consequently bounded by a finite constant times the measurable indicator 1_Q; continuous sections are measurable, and this bound has finite integral because μ(Q)=(2R)^n. Thus all listed sections are absolutely integrable. The same boundedness argument on Q×K for any compact subinterval K⊂int(J) proves all the asserted uniform bounds.

produces.statement: For these C,R,J,Q, μ(Q)=(2R)^n<∞ and all positive-order derivatives of u vanish on (R^n\C)×int(J). The functions e,e_t are smooth. For every r∈int(J), the spatial sections e, e_t, u_t·u_tt and, for every j∈{1,…,n}, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), evaluated at r, are continuous, zero outside C and absolutely integrable. These scalar functions have finite bounds on Q×K for every compact K⊂int(J).

argument.text: The properties in F002 hold for the witnesses C,R chosen above. In particular t0∈int(J), so e(·,t0) is integrable. Package their existence, with the displayed formulas J=[t0/2,3t0/2] and Q=[-R,R]^n, and quantify over arbitrary t0>0. This proves all the asserted support and boundedness properties, including integrability at every positive time. The choices of C and R remain existential for each time window.

locals.declaration: Choose C and R from N002 for t0, with its common support and boundedness properties.
Choose R jointly with C as in N002, so C⊂(-R,R)^n.
Choose B≥0 bounding |e_t| on Q×[t0-η,t0+η], using F002.
Fix an arbitrary spatial point x for the difference-quotient estimate.
Fix an arbitrary real increment h.
Fix an arbitrary sequence of real increments hseq.

locals.type: sequence of real functions on R^n

argument.text: Fix t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and choose C,R from N002 for this t0; put Q=[-R,R]^n. N002 gives finiteness of the spatial energy integrals for every positive time, so the guarded definition of E is available. H001 gives the finite coordinate range. H002 gives the product rule and equality ∂_t∂_{x_j}u=∂_{x_j}u_t. Hence pointwise on the full domain, e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. By N002 these terms are spatially integrable at all times in int(J).

produces.statement: On R^n×(0,∞), e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t; all terms are spatially integrable at times in int(J), and e is smooth.

argument.text: Set η=t0/4>0. Then [t0-η,t0+η]⊂int(J). By F001 and N002, e_t is continuous on the compact Q×[t0-η,t0+η], so its absolute value has a finite nonnegative bound. Consequently there exists B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B on that box. The compactness and boundedness facts used here are the standard extreme-value property for continuous real functions on a compact finite-dimensional box.

produces.statement: There exists B≥0 such that for all x∈Q and r∈[t0-η,t0+η], |e_t(x,r)|≤B.

argument.text: Choose B from F002. Fix x∈R^n and a real h, and temporarily assume L1: 0<|h|<η. For x∈Q, apply M002 to the real function r↦e(x,r) on the interval with endpoints min(t0,t0+h) and max(t0,t0+h), and derivative r↦e_t(x,r). Both endpoints and the full interval lie in [t0-η,t0+η]. F001 supplies differentiability and continuity there, and F002 bounds the intermediate derivative. The theorem's slope is (e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h also when h<0, because reversing both differences changes neither quotient. Thus its absolute value is at most B. If x∉Q, N002 makes both densities zero and gives the same estimate with right side zero. Discharge L1 and quantify x,h: for all x and all 0<|h|<η, |(e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h|≤B 1_Q(x). The right side is integrable by μ(Q)=(2R)^n<∞, from N002.

produces.statement: For all x∈R^n and real h with 0<|h|<η, |(e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h|≤B 1_Q(x), and the function x↦B 1_Q(x) is μ-integrable.

argument.text: Fix an arbitrary real sequence hseq and temporarily assume L2: 0<|hseq(k)|<η for every k and hseq(k)→0. Define Fseq(k)(y)=(e(y,t0+hseq(k))-e(y,t0))/hseq(k). These are continuous real spatial functions, hence μ-almost everywhere strongly measurable. By F003 they are dominated pointwise by B 1_Q, which is integrable. Smoothness in F001 gives pointwise convergence Fseq(k)(y)→e_t(y,t0). Apply M001 with spatial Lebesgue measure μ and real codomain: ∫Fseq(k) dμ→∫e_t(y,t0) dμ. For each k, the two densities are integrable by N002; integral linearity and scalar multiplication identify ∫Fseq(k) dμ=(E(t0+hseq(k))-E(t0))/hseq(k). Thus the energy difference quotients converge to ∫e_t(y,t0) dμ along this sequence.

produces.statement: (E(t0+hseq(k))-E(t0))/hseq(k) tends to ∫_{R^n} e_t(y,t0) dμ(y) as k→∞.

argument.text: Discharge L2 in F004 and quantify the arbitrary sequence. Any sequence of nonzero real increments tending to zero eventually satisfies |h|<η, so discarding its finite initial part yields the same limit. The sequential criterion for limits in R now gives the full two-sided difference-quotient limit at zero. Explicitly, if that limit failed, a fixed positive error could be attained by nonzero increments arbitrarily close to zero; choosing one at distance less than min(η,1/(k+1)) for each k would contradict the just-proved sequence limit. Thus E is differentiable at t0 and E'(t0)=∫ e_t(x,t0) dx. Substitute F001 and use finite linearity of the integral; every summand is absolutely integrable by N002. This yields E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx, at time t0. The pointwise formula, finiteness, and arbitrary choice of t0 prove all asserted differentiation identities and finiteness clauses.

applications.bindings: Set f(r)=e(x,r), d(r)=e_t(x,r); a=min(t0,t0+h), b=max(t0,t0+h). Use the real functions extended arbitrarily outside positive times, which does not affect this interval.
hypothesis_checks: L1 gives h≠0 and hence a<b; all quantities are real, and a,b lie within [t0-η,t0+η]⊂(0,∞).
F001 gives smoothness of e, so r↦e(x,r) is continuous on [a,b].
F001 gives derivative e_t(x,r) at every interior r; F002 bounds its absolute value at the intermediate point when x∈Q.

applications.bindings: Set A=R^n with its Borel measurable structure, ν=μ, V=R, F=Fseq, f(y)=e_t(y,t0), and bound b(y)=B 1_Q(y).
hypothesis_checks: R^n is a measurable Euclidean space with Lebesgue measure μ (D005); R is a real normed vector space.
Under L2 all increments are nonzero and t0+hseq(k)>0. Each Fseq(k) is continuous in space by F001, hence almost everywhere strongly measurable.
F003 proves integrability of B 1_Q, using finite μ(Q) in N002.
F003 applies pointwise to h=hseq(k) under L2, and supplies the domination for every k.
Under L2, hseq(k)→0 and hseq(k)≠0. The time derivative of e from F001 gives pointwise difference-quotient convergence to e_t(y,t0).

locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary spatial coordinate j∈{1,…,n}.
Choose C from N002 for t0 together with its R.
Choose R jointly with C from N002, with C⊂(-R,R)^n.
I_j(y,z) has coordinate j equal to z and its other coordinates equal to those of y, in increasing coordinate order.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and j∈{1,…,n}; H001 supplies n≥1. Choose C,R from N002 for J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and set Q=[-R,R]^n. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). By H002 it is smooth. Its derivative, by the product rule, is ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u at time t0. By N002, both summands, g and its derivative are integrable and vanish off C. Since C⊂int(Q), the complement of C is an open neighborhood of the boundary of Q, and g vanishes there. In particular the two j-coordinate face values are zero.

produces.statement: At time t0, ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. The functions g, ∂_{x_j}g and these two summands are smooth, integrable, zero outside C, and g vanishes near the boundary of Q.

argument.text: Use the coordinate insertion I_j(y,z), with coordinate j equal to z and remaining coordinates given by y. Fix arbitrary y∈[-R,R]^(n-1), and define fline(z)=g(I_j(y,z)), dline(z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). By F001 and the coordinate chain rule, fline is smooth, its derivative is dline, and both endpoint values fline(-R),fline(R) are zero. The continuous derivative dline is bounded and integrable on [-R,R]. Apply M003 with real codomain and a=-R,b=R: ∫_{-R..R}dline(z) dz=fline(R)-fline(-R)=0. Endpoints are null for one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so the same holds for the integral over [-R,R]. Since y was arbitrary, the integral in coordinate j of ∂_{x_j}g is zero for every choice of remaining box coordinates.

Set v(y,z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). Split Q into its remaining n-1 coordinates and coordinate j, with their restricted Lebesgue measures. This is the same measure as μ restricted to Q under I_j: on every coordinate subrectangle both give the product of its side lengths, and these rectangles determine the finite measures; the coordinate reordering merely reorders these factors. Both restricted measures are finite, hence s-finite. The function v is continuous and bounded on the compact product box, so it is integrable for that finite product measure. Apply M004 to v with the remaining coordinates as the outer variable and coordinate j as the inner variable. This gives ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{[-R,R]^(n-1)}(∫_{[-R,R]}∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)) dz) dy=0 by F002. For n=1 the remaining-coordinate space is R^0, a singleton with its zero-dimensional Lebesgue measure of mass one, so the identical formula reduces to the one-dimensional integral; no exceptional empty-coordinate case is omitted.

By F001 all terms vanish off C⊂Q, so F003 gives ∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}g dx=0. The product identity in F001 and integral linearity, justified by absolute integrability of both summands, give 0=∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0) dx+∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx. Symmetry of the dot product and rearrangement yield ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, with all terms at time t0. Quantify over the arbitrary t0 and j to conclude the asserted integration-by-parts formula and its finiteness assertions.

applications.bindings: Take V=R, f=fline, d=dline, a=-R,b=R for each fixed y∈[-R,R]^(n-1).
hypothesis_checks: R with its usual norm is a complete real normed vector space.
F001 makes g smooth; the affine coordinate line gives continuity of fline on [-R,R].
The coordinate chain rule applied to the smooth g in F001 gives derivative dline at every interior point.
The continuous dline on the compact interval is bounded and measurable, hence interval integrable.

applications.bindings: Take A=R^(n-1) with Lebesgue measure restricted to [-R,R]^(n-1), B=R with Lebesgue measure restricted to [-R,R], V=R, and f=v. Identify this coordinate product with Q by the insertion map I_j as proved in S003.
hypothesis_checks: Both Euclidean spaces are measurable and both restricted coordinate measures are finite, thus s-finite; if n=1 the first is the singleton measure of mass one.
R is a normed additive commutative group and a normed vector space over R.
By F001, ∂_{x_j}g is continuous on compact Q; after insertion it is measurable and bounded on the product box, whose measure is (2R)^n<∞ by N002. Hence v is integrable for the product measure.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary t0>0. H001 gives finitely many spatial coordinates, and H002 supplies the derivative notation. N002 proves e(·,t0) integrable and thereby makes the guarded definition of E available. N003 proves differentiability of E at t0 and the absolutely finite identity E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. Apply N004 at t0 for each of the finitely many spatial indices to replace each second integral by -∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx.

produces.statement: E is differentiable at t0 and E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·u_tt(x,t0) dx-2∑_{j=1}^n∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx; all terms are absolutely finite.

argument.text: By the definition Δ_xu=∑_{j=1}^n∂_{x_jx_j}u and finite linearity of these integrable terms, F001 becomes E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)-Δ_xu(x,t0)) dx. N001 states that this integrand is zero pointwise, hence E'(t0)=0. Since t0 was arbitrary, E is differentiable on (0,∞) and has zero derivative at every positive time. N002 already supplies integrability for every such time.

produces.statement: For every t>0, e(·,t) is integrable, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0.

argument.text: For completeness take any 0<a0<b0. F002 gives differentiability, hence continuity, of E at all points of [a0,b0], and derivative zero on (a0,b0). Apply M002 with f equal to E on positive times, derivative function zero there, and endpoints a0,b0 (extend f arbitrarily to nonpositive arguments). It yields (E(b0)-E(a0))/(b0-a0)=0; since b0-a0>0, E(b0)=E(a0). Equality is automatic for coincident times, and for reversed positive times interchange their roles. Therefore E is constant on (0,∞). Together with F002 and the definition of E this proves the complete conclusion with coefficient one on both squared norms and without any time-zero assertion.

applications.bindings: Set f(r)=E(r) for r>0 and extend it arbitrarily outside (0,∞); set d(r)=0, a=a0, b=b0.
hypothesis_checks: F002 proves differentiability of E throughout the positive interval, which implies continuity on [a0,b0].
F002 proves that for every r∈(a0,b0), E has derivative zero, exactly d(r).
